newsitem.title: CANADA: Inco talks in Manitoba break down.
newsitem.headline: Inco talks in Manitoba break down.

text.p: Talks between Inco Ltd and its locked out workers in Thompson, Manitoba have broken down, the company and union said on Monday.
"Talks broke down last night," said Inco spokesman Dan McSweeney. "We are unable to resolve the outstanding issues."
Inco locked out its employees on Sunday night after the workers voted 71 percent against Inco's final contract offer.
The lockout would not affect the supply of nickel to Inco's customers, McSweeney said.
Inco produces about 100 million pounds of nickel a year from the Thompson area in northern Manitoba.
McSweeney would not say how long the company could maintain an uninterrupted supply in the face of a lockout.
United Steelworkers union spokesman Bob Desjarlais said production at Thompson was essential to Inco.
"They had a tremendous amount of nickel sales on the computers here in this facility," he said in a phone interview. "They needed to get the nickel out of here."
Desjarlais said talks broke down early Monday over wages and scheduling issues.
No further talks were scheduled and workers were picketing the facility, the union and company said.
"We are prepared to bargain any time any where," said Desjarlais, who represents 1,327 workers at local 6166.
"We were prepared to work under the old collective agreement until we reached a new one. Inco flatly rejected that."
Inco said its final offer was fair and the company did not want to continue to operate without a contract.
Neither side would say how long they thought the dispute would continue.
"We are always willing to talk to the union," Inco's McSweeney said.
Workers objected to a company proposal to work shifts up to 12 hours long and a pay freeze in the last two years of a three-year contract, Desjarlais said.
